subtopic_detail: When contraception can be stopped in a woman using progestogen only pills at fifty three
stem:
A 53 year old woman attends your general practice for a repeat prescription. She has taken a progestogen only pill continuously for nine years and has had no bleeding at all for the past four years.

She asks whether she still needs contraception, saying she is certain she has gone through the menopause and that her friend was told to have a blood test to prove it. She has no hot flushes and no vaginal dryness. She is a non smoker, her blood pressure is normal, and she has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism or breast cancer.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 70 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 15 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 26 kg/m2, no abnormality on abdominal or pelvic examination
data_table.Contraceptive history: Progestogen only pill for nine years, amenorrhoeic for four years, no missed pills
data_table.Other: Non smoker, no vasomotor symptoms, cervical screening up to date and negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Continue the pill until she is 55 and then stop it
options.rationale: Contraception is recommended until age 55, by which age natural conception is exceptionally rare, and it can then be stopped without any hormonal testing. Amenorrhoea on a progestogen only pill is caused by the pill itself and cannot be used as evidence that ovulation has ceased. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception in the perimenopause)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception in the perimenopause

options.text: Stop the pill now given four years without any bleeding
options.rationale: Amenorrhoea is an expected effect of continuous progestogen and does not indicate loss of ovarian function, so stopping on that basis leaves her at risk of a late and unintended pregnancy. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception in the perimenopause)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception in the perimenopause

options.text: Check two follicle stimulating hormone levels and then stop
options.rationale: Measuring follicle stimulating hormone is an option in women aged 50 or over using progestogen only methods, but results fluctuate widely in the perimenopause and a raised value does not exclude a subsequent ovulation. Continuing to 55 avoids the ambiguity altogether. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception in the perimenopause)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception in the perimenopause

options.text: Change to the combined oral contraceptive pill until age 55
options.rationale: Combined hormonal contraception is generally avoided from age 50 because the cardiovascular and thromboembolic risks outweigh its benefits, and she has no indication for oestrogen. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception in the perimenopause)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception in the perimenopause

options.text: Stop the pill and use condoms alone until she turns 55
options.rationale: Barrier methods are far less effective than a progestogen only pill she is already taking without problems, and there is no clinical reason to downgrade her contraceptive efficacy at this stage. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception in the perimenopause)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception in the perimenopause

explanation.summary: Fertility falls sharply but does not disappear in the late forties and early fifties, and unintended pregnancy at this age carries high maternal and foetal risk. The simplest and safest rule is to continue contraception until age 55, at which point it can be stopped regardless of bleeding pattern and without hormonal testing. Amenorrhoea while taking a progestogen only method is caused by the method and says nothing about ovarian activity, which is the central trap in this scenario. Combined hormonal contraception is generally discontinued at age 50 in favour of progestogen only or intrauterine methods.
key_points: Age 55 is the point at which contraception can be stopped without testing
Amenorrhoea on progestogen is method induced and is not evidence of menopause
Follicle stimulating hormone testing is optional from age 50 on progestogen only methods but is unreliable in isolation
A levonorgestrel intrauterine system fitted at 45 or older may be retained until 55 if used for contraception alone
explanation.pearls: If she later needs hormone replacement therapy for vasomotor symptoms, remember that standard hormone replacement is not contraceptive: she needs a separate contraceptive method alongside it until 55.

sources.label: Family Planning Australia: Contraception in the perimenopause
Australasian Menopause Society: Contraception and the perimenopause

subtopic_detail: Severe hot flushes in a woman taking tamoxifen after breast cancer
stem:
A 49 year old woman attends your general practice with severe hot flushes occurring around fifteen times a day and waking her four or five times each night. She has been exhausted for months and has started declining work and social commitments.

She completed treatment for an oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer eighteen months ago and takes tamoxifen. Her periods stopped during chemotherapy. She has tried reducing caffeine and alcohol, layered clothing and a bedroom fan without benefit. She has no depression on assessment, no vaginal bleeding, and her mood is low only in proportion to the sleep deprivation. She is not taking any antidepressant and has no history of seizures.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 15 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 25 kg/m2, no lymphadenopathy, surgical breast examination unremarkable, no abnormality on abdominal examination
data_table.Symptom burden: Approximately fifteen daytime flushes and four to five night time waking episodes daily
data_table.Oncology history: Oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer treated eighteen months ago, currently on tamoxifen
data_table.Measures already tried: Caffeine and alcohol reduction, clothing layering, bedroom cooling, without benefit

options.text: Start systemic oestrogen therapy at the lowest effective dose
options.rationale: Systemic oestrogen is contraindicated after an oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer because of the risk of stimulating recurrence, regardless of how severe the vasomotor symptoms are. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Non hormonal treatments for menopausal symptoms)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Non hormonal treatments for menopausal symptoms

options.text: Start venlafaxine rather than any hormonal preparation
options.rationale: Venlafaxine has the best evidence among non hormonal agents for reducing vasomotor symptom frequency and severity and is a preferred choice in women taking tamoxifen because it does not meaningfully inhibit the enzyme that converts tamoxifen to its active metabolite. Her symptom burden is well past the point at which lifestyle measures alone suffice. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Non hormonal treatments for menopausal symptoms)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Non hormonal treatments for menopausal symptoms

options.text: Start paroxetine as the non hormonal agent with best evidence
options.rationale: Paroxetine does reduce flushes but is a potent inhibitor of cytochrome P450 2D6, which converts tamoxifen to its active metabolite, so it risks reducing the effectiveness of her cancer treatment. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Non hormonal treatments for menopausal symptoms)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Non hormonal treatments for menopausal symptoms

options.text: Recommend a phytoestrogen preparation available over the counter
options.rationale: Evidence of benefit is weak and inconsistent, and preparations with oestrogenic activity are generally avoided after hormone receptor positive breast cancer. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Non hormonal treatments for menopausal symptoms)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Non hormonal treatments for menopausal symptoms

options.text: Continue lifestyle measures alone and review her again in six months
options.rationale: Lifestyle measures have already been tried without benefit and are insufficient for a symptom burden that is disrupting sleep nightly and causing her to withdraw from work and social life. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Non hormonal treatments for menopausal symptoms)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Non hormonal treatments for menopausal symptoms

explanation.summary: Vasomotor symptoms after breast cancer treatment are often more severe than those of natural menopause, because ovarian function is abruptly lost through chemotherapy and endocrine therapy adds its own effect. Systemic oestrogen is contraindicated after hormone receptor positive disease, so management relies on non hormonal options, of which the serotonin noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors and gabapentin have the best evidence. The specific pharmacological trap is that some selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, particularly paroxetine and fluoxetine, are potent inhibitors of cytochrome P450 2D6 and reduce conversion of tamoxifen to its active metabolite. Venlafaxine and desvenlafaxine have minimal effect on that enzyme and are therefore preferred in women taking tamoxifen.
key_points: Systemic oestrogen is contraindicated after oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer
Paroxetine and fluoxetine inhibit cytochrome P450 2D6 and can undermine tamoxifen
Venlafaxine, desvenlafaxine and gabapentin are the preferred non hormonal options
Cognitive behavioural therapy has evidence for reducing the impact of flushes
explanation.pearls: Vaginal oestrogen is a separate question from systemic therapy: low dose vaginal preparations for genitourinary symptoms are often acceptable after discussion with the treating oncologist, even in women for whom systemic oestrogen is firmly contraindicated.

sources.label: Australasian Menopause Society: Non hormonal treatments for menopausal symptoms

subtopic_detail: Duration of anticoagulation after a pulmonary embolism at thirty weeks
stem:
You are the obstetric medicine registrar reviewing a 33 year old woman who was diagnosed with a segmental pulmonary embolism at 30 weeks and started on therapeutic enoxaparin. She is now 38 weeks and well, with no chest pain and no breathlessness.

She has no personal history of previous thrombosis, no known thrombophilia and no family history of clotting problems. She asks how long she will need the injections after the baby is born, and whether she can change to tablets so she can stop injecting herself. She intends to breastfeed. A birth plan is being made for induction at 39 weeks.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 17 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 142 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Chest clear, calves soft and non tender, symphysis fundal height 38 cm
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count and renal function within normal limits, platelets 232 x10^9/L, no thrombophilia identified
data_table.Treatment: Therapeutic enoxaparin since 30 weeks, well tolerated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about the duration of treatment?

options.text: Stop the anticoagulation once she has given birth safely
options.rationale: The six weeks after birth are the period of greatest risk because of venous stasis, vessel injury and the procoagulant state, so stopping at delivery removes protection precisely when it is most needed. (Source: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Change to a direct oral anticoagulant as soon as she delivers
options.rationale: Direct oral anticoagulants are not recommended during breastfeeding because of limited safety data and measurable excretion into milk, so they are avoided in a woman who intends to breastfeed. (Source: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Continue therapeutic anticoagulation for six weeks postpartum
options.rationale: Pregnancy associated venous thromboembolism is treated for a minimum of three months in total and for at least six weeks after birth, whichever is longer, because the postpartum period carries the highest thrombotic risk of the whole pregnancy. She was diagnosed at 30 weeks, so six weeks postpartum takes her past the three month minimum. (Source: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Reduce to a prophylactic dose for six weeks after she delivers
options.rationale: Dose reduction applies to women receiving prophylaxis for risk factors, not to treatment of an established event within the same pregnancy, which requires therapeutic intensity for the full course. (Source: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Continue therapeutic anticoagulation indefinitely from now on
options.rationale: Lifelong treatment is reserved for unprovoked recurrent events or high risk thrombophilia. Pregnancy is a transient major provoking factor, so a defined course is appropriate with prophylaxis considered in future pregnancies. (Source: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy and the puerperium

explanation.summary: Venous thromboembolism occurring in pregnancy is treated with therapeutic low molecular weight heparin for at least three months in total and for a minimum of six weeks after birth, whichever period is longer. The postpartum rule exists because thrombotic risk peaks in the puerperium rather than falling at delivery. Warfarin is compatible with breastfeeding and can be used postnatally, but direct oral anticoagulants are avoided because they are excreted in breast milk with limited safety data. Pregnancy counts as a transient provoking factor, so indefinite anticoagulation is not required, but prophylaxis is recommended in subsequent pregnancies and the puerperium.
key_points: At least three months total and at least six weeks postpartum, whichever is longer
Risk of thrombosis is highest in the first six weeks after birth, not during pregnancy
Low molecular weight heparin and warfarin are both compatible with breastfeeding; direct oral anticoagulants are not
A pregnancy associated event indicates thromboprophylaxis in future pregnancies
explanation.pearls: Plan the peripartum interruption explicitly: therapeutic low molecular weight heparin is usually withheld for 24 hours before planned birth or neuraxial block, and a woman on treatment dose should have a documented plan converting her to a shorter acting strategy as induction approaches.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy and the puerperium
